entities.name: Ryuk ransomware
entities.evidence: Ryuk ransomware was first observed in August 2018 [1].

entities.name: Hermes 2.1
entities.evidence: Ryuk is a variant of the Hermes 2.1 ransomware, sold on the underground forum exploit.in from February 2017 by the cybercriminal group CryptoTech for around 300 dollars [2].

entities.name: CryptoTech
entities.evidence: The cybercriminal group CryptoTech confirmed that it was behind the ransomware and announced the forthcoming release of a new version of Hermes.

entities.name: Bluenoroff
entities.evidence: A connection with the tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) of the Bluenoroff intrusion set, reportedly linked to North Korea, had been momentarily established by some editors.

entities.name: ANSSI
entities.evidence: A Ryuk sample with worm-like capabilities allowing it to spread automatically within networks it infects, was discovered during an incident response handled by the ANSSI in early 2021.

entities.name: Deloitte
entities.evidence: Deloitte researchers believe Ryuk is sold as a toolkit to attacker groups.

entities.name: Ahnlab
entities.evidence: Ahnlab is a South Korean IT threat analysis and response company.

entities.name: Ryuk ransomware
entities.evidence: Ryuk is not officially a RaaS. However, it appears that several different attackers are involved in infection chains leading to the deployment of Ryuk.

entities.name: Hermes 2.1
entities.evidence: The Hermes kit sold on the Dark Web did not contain any exploitation tool, forcing its buyers to compromise the victims using their own resources or those of an intermediary.

entities.name: FIN6
entities.evidence: FIN6 or affiliated parties would clearly have been involved in Ryuk incidents in 2019 in which no intermediate payload of the type seen with previous loaders was observed.

entities.name: UNC1878
entities.evidence: According to FireEye, UNC1878 is responsible for 83% of Ryuk infections in 2020 and is not believed to exfiltrate any information, unlike other Ryuk operators that may exfiltrate internal reconnaissance information from their victims’ networks.

entities.name: T1059.001
entities.evidence: The Ryuk ransomware remains particularly active in the second half of 2020. It differs from most other ransomwares in that at least one of its operators attacked hospitals during a pandemic, the absence of a dedicated data disclosure site and the extreme speed of execution (around a few hours) of the Bazar-Ryuk chain of infection.

entities.name: Wake-On-LAN
entities.evidence: Ryuk looks for network shares on the victim IT infrastructure. To do so, some private IP ranges are scanned: ... Before this scan step, Ryuk reads through the victim’s ARP table and sends a Wake-On-LAN paquet to each host.

entities.name: SMB
entities.evidence: Ryuk looks for network shares on the victim IT infrastructure. To do so, some private IP ranges are scanned: ... For each identified host, Ryuk will attempt to mount possible network shares using SMB enumeration.

entities.name: schtasks.exe
entities.evidence: The scheduled task is created through a call to the schtasks.exe system tool, a native-Windows tool.

entities.name: icacls
entities.evidence: The malware can launch icacls <path> /grant Everyone:F /T /C /Q to delete every access-based restrictions on files and directories.

entities.name: wordpad.exe
entities.evidence: The fake DLL is locally launched through a scheduled task executing wordpad.exe <random>.dll.
